summary:
Erzincan province sits under the Turkish national legal framework with no province-specific ordinance, incident or court decision on record, so the national picture governs what a trans visitor faces here. The framework is contradictory on its face: homosexuality has been decriminalised since 1858, gender-reassignment surgery has been legal since 1988, and discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity is prohibited by law. Those provisions coexist with a documented pattern of enforcement hostility.

Same-sex relationships, marriage, civil unions and same-sex adoption receive no legal recognition, and LGBTI people are barred from serving openly in the military. In ILGA-Europe's 2026 Rainbow Europe ranking Türkiye placed 47th of 49, ahead only of Azerbaijan and Russia.

The sharpest threat to a visitor comes from a leaked draft of the 11th Judicial Package, reported by Human Rights Watch on 29 October 2025. The omnibus draft would amend the penal and civil codes to criminalise conduct deemed "contrary to biological sex and general morality", carrying up to three years' imprisonment, and would sharply restrict gender-affirming healthcare by raising the minimum age to 25 and imposing onerous eligibility conditions. The package would allow criminal charges against both trans people and the professionals providing their care. The government's stated justification is protecting "the family" and "public morals". The same draft carries unrelated measures including longer child sentences and online-content removal.

In early 2026 the government was reported to be considering going further and criminalising public advocacy of "behaviour contrary to biological sex and general morality". The legislative status of either measure is not established in the sources available here.

Pride marches have been banned and forcibly dispersed by the authorities since 2015, using tear gas, water cannons and mass detentions. ILGA-Europe reported on 7 December 2020 that 19 human rights defenders faced prosecution for taking part in a peaceful Pride march at Middle East Technical University in Ankara in May 2019, which shows that even a campus march can draw criminal charges. That exposure for LGBT advocacy is the national freedom-of-assembly climate a visitor in Erzincan would be judged against.

Under the national framework, checkpoint and identity-document checks are the recurring point of contact between a trans visitor and the state. Foreign nationals are required to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira and warnings of detention for non-compliance, and any stop becomes an occasion on which documents are compared against presentation. Regular police identity checks (GBT) applied to trans women in Istanbul through 2025 illustrate how such encounters are used for documentation even without charges.
tangentialFactors:
Erzincan is a province rather than a distinct legal regime, so the turbulence recorded elsewhere in Türkiye is the background here rather than a local finding. Reported enforcement in Istanbul — roughly 20 trans women stopped in Beyoğlu during 2025 and held at Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station for GBT checks — is evidence of national practice, not of anything specific to Erzincan.

The 2025 figures compiled by Kaos GL give a sense of scale: 313 recorded violations in one year, roughly two and a half times the 2024 total, with 299 detention decisions, 256 through formal channels and 43 taken off the record. Six deaths were linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three classified by rights organisations as hate killings, with transgender people disproportionately affected.

The pending draft package has shaped behaviour before passage. Reporting on Istanbul stops in 2025 quotes women who noted that the new law had not been passed even as enforcement was already being applied to them, and legal experts cited in that reporting argue that such checks violate Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights.

Care policy is tightening independently of the draft package. A Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025, following a Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular that added "gender reassignment" as an official reason for medical-board reports, barred hospitals from recording the "other" option and required e-reports to be issued, which risks profiling trans patients in official records and restricting access to transition care.
localsOnly:
Residents of Erzincan live under the same statutory discrimination prohibition on sexual orientation and gender identity grounds that applies nationally, but that protection has not translated into recognition: no marriage, civil union or joint adoption is available to same-sex partners, and open service in the military is barred for LGBTI people.

Gender-reassignment surgery has been legal in Türkiye since 1988. Access for residents is governed by medical-board procedures, and the September 2025 Health Ministry regulation on reporting requirements affects how transition care is recorded in official systems.

Trans prisoners are placed by registered sex rather than gender identity. The death of the trans prisoner Poyraz at Sincan Women's Prison on 1 December 2025 prompted demands from Human Rights Association branches in Istanbul, Ankara, Izmir, Diyarbakır, Mersin and Aydın for an independent investigation; accounts from other trans prisoners and lawyers reported four transgender inmates sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, delayed medical staff, prosecutors entering two days later, and witness statements not taken. The case was raised in parliament by opposition MP Sevda Karaca on 12 December 2025.

Prison conditions for LGBT detainees are governed by segregation and isolation rather than gender-matched placement, according to the Prison Insider country profile prepared with the Civil Society in the Penal System Association using ILGA World data. It documents arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto solitary confinement with restricted access to healthcare, refusals of hospital transfer, binary administration with no staff training on LGBTI needs, transfers that disrupt visits and solidarity networks, and complaints procedures that are ineffective and can attract further violence.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Erzincan-specific incident, ordinance or court decision was located in the sources used for this record. The province is treated here as an instance of the national framework, and any local variation in policing or facilities practice remains unresolved.

The legislative status of the 11th Judicial Package is unresolved. Human Rights Watch reported the leaked draft on 29 October 2025 and described measures under consideration; whether the package was introduced, amended or enacted after that date is not sourced here. The same applies to the reported early-2026 proposal to criminalise public advocacy.

The outcome of the prosecution of the 19 Pride marchers in Ankara is not stated in the available sources beyond ILGA-Europe's December 2020 call for acquittal.

Whether the discrimination prohibition on sexual orientation and gender identity grounds has been successfully enforced by a Turkish court is not evidenced in this inventory.
